content: The Nix-TB study presented data on the use of linezolid in patients with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB). Among the 109 patients included in the study, anemia was reported in 37% of cases, while peripheral sensory neuropathy was observed in 69% of patients. Pharmacokinetic modeling indicated that linezolid exhibits nonlinear pharmacokinetics in XDR-TB patients, and individual linezolid concentration-time profiles were identified as the best predictors of toxicity. Higher toxicity rates were associated with higher total daily doses of linezolid, with similar toxicity rates observed between twice-daily (BID) and once-daily (QD) dosing regimens. Management of anemia during linezolid treatment involves close monitoring of hemoglobin levels during the first four weeks of therapy. A hemoglobin increase of more than 10% from baseline should prompt a reduction in the linezolid dose, as hemoglobin levels typically recover well following dose adjustments. Peripheral neuropathy, when it occurs, is reversible in most patients within three months, but it requires close monitoring. Thrombocytopenia, while a potential side effect, is not considered a major concern with high-dose linezolid in XDR-TB patients. The study also highlighted the high rate of adverse events associated with the BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid). Serious adverse events, including hospitalizations and life-threatening events, were reported in 25% of participants, and 49% experienced at least one Grade 3–4 adverse event. Linezolid-related adverse events led to discontinuation of the drug in 32% of patients, particularly at the initial dose of 1200 mg/day. Only 18% of patients were able to complete a full course of linezolid at this dose. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) noted the challenges in comparing adverse event rates across studies due to differences in adverse event ascertainment, assessment, and reporting. They also acknowledged the uncertainty in the evidence regarding the reversibility of peripheral neuropathy, which could be either complete or incomplete. The potentially debilitating effects of irreversible peripheral neuropathy were a significant concern for both patients and clinicians. The GDG also considered the issue of male infertility, which was observed in animal models and raised concerns about its potential impact on patients and their families. Monitoring infertility in programmatic settings was deemed challenging, and additional human sperm studies recommended by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration are planned but were not available at the time of the meeting. The GDG emphasized that infertility is a serious issue, particularly given the limited treatment options available at the time the Nix-TB study began. The GDG evaluated the desirable effects of treatment success, which were higher in the intervention groups compared to comparator groups across all assessed treatment outcomes. However, the high rate of adverse events associated with the BPaL regimen, particularly those related to linezolid, was a significant concern. The panel acknowledged the difficulty in balancing the benefits of treatment success with the burden of adverse effects, including the substantial pill burden associated with longer regimens for multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB).
